looking-at-the-shore-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for one part of the star-shaped animal. Then think about where seawater stays when the tide has gone out.

guitar-to-gathering-4.solvingTip: Start with what the player uses to hear the notes. Then look for the small part they turn and the word for how high or deep a note sounds.

garden-harvest-baskets-4.solvingTip: Start with the tool that loosens the mound. Once the potatoes are out, look for the word for one of the small buds on the surface.

pantry-packets-and-labels-5.solvingTip: Look for the clue for the bowl's bottom first. Then use crossings to work out what the towel does against the counter.

notes.DAMP: A damp towel has some water in it without being soaked. A wrung-out cloth is one example.
notes.GRIP: The towel grips the counter in the sense of resisting a slide. Neither the towel nor the bowl needs a handle for that kind of grip.

clues.COUNTER: Flat kitchen surface where you set a mixing bowl
clues.REST: Sit on a support, as a bowl does on a towel

small-actions-at-the-serving-table.solvingTip: Try the clue for the rounded serving dish. Its letters can help with the word for the part of the spoon a guest can lift.

notes.RIM: Think of where your lips touch a cup. The bowl's rim is the same kind of border, and here it supports the spoon.
notes.REST: Rest is a verb in this clue. Like a book resting on a shelf, the spoon stays up because something underneath supports it.

watching-at-the-pond-4.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for what people breathe. Then try the actions a bubble can take on its way up and at the surface.

notes.BUBBLES: A bubble has air inside it. A ripple is movement along the water and has no pocket of air.
notes.BURST: When a bubble bursts, its thin boundary breaks and the air escapes. The word describes what happens to the bubble itself.

clues.RINGS: Circles that spread outward on the water

watching-at-the-pond-5.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the animal first. Then look for the words that track its movement up and back down.

notes.RINGS: The rings are a shape made by moving water. They start together at the place the fish came up and spread outward.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward, as ripples do on water

breakfast-on-the-griddle-5.solvingTip: Find the short clue for what goes inside the flat bread. Then use its crossings on the clue for bringing one side over.

notes.TORTILLA: The bread needs to bend without cracking to hold the eggs. A crisp tortilla chip is made from similar bread but won't fold that way.
notes.FOLD: A fold brings part of the tortilla over the eggs. A roll would keep turning the tortilla around the filling.

clues.WRAP: Bring the flat bread around the eggs

water-edges-after-weather-4.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the still body of water. Then try the moving water that enters it.

notes.RIPPLES: A ripple travels along the top of the water. The creek can keep flowing into the pond after the small waves have spread out.
notes.CREEK: The important word in the clue is flowing. Even a narrow creek has water moving along a channel, while the pond is mostly still.

animals-around-the-farmyard-2.solvingTip: Begin with the clue for the shallow container. Then try the short action the birds make with their heads at the water.

notes.BILL: A duck's bill is its beak. Here it goes into the water, so this is the animal meaning of the word you might also see on a request for payment.
notes.SPLASH: A duck can dip its bill in very gently. To splash, it moves enough to send some water out of the pan.

clues.FEATHERS: Covering on a bird, including the long ones on its wings
clues.PAN: Shallow metal container that holds water for the ducks

eating-at-the-diner-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue about what rises from the hot cereal. Then use the letters to find the grain named in the dish.

notes.WHEAT: Wheat names the grain that is milled to make the cereal. The finished dish and the grain have separate clues.
notes.CEREAL: Cereal can be served hot or cold. The steam in this diner scene points to a cooked bowl, like oatmeal or hot wheat cereal.

clues.STEAM: What rises visibly from a bowl of very hot cereal
clues.LUMP: Small clump in cereal that should be smooth

neighborhood-pet-care.solvingTip: Try the clue for the wet dirt first. Then look for the cloth you would reach for at the door.

notes.PAWS: A paw print is the mark a paw can leave. The towel dries the dog's feet to keep those marks off the floor.
notes.MUD: Mud has soil in it as well as water. A dog's wet paws can leave a puddle without leaving any dirt.

clues.TOWEL: Absorbent cloth used to dry a dog's wet feet

classic-movie-settings-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the water falling from the clouds. Use those letters to find the cover carried above the dancer.

clues.COAT: Outer garment worn over your clothes in the rain
clues.TAP: Light strike a dancer makes with a shoe

notes.SHOE: A tap shoe makes its sound when the metal under it strikes the ground. The toe and heel give the dancer different ways to make a beat.

old-shop-tools.solvingTip: Try the clue for the person behind the counter. Then picture what a waiting customer does to get that person's attention.

clues.TAP: Give the bell a light strike with a finger

notes.RING: Ring is a verb here. A small tap is the action your finger makes, and ringing is what the bell does in response.

picnic-band-sounds-2.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the small flat pieces around the instrument. Then look for the sound they make when they move.

clues.FRAME: Outer ring that holds the tambourine's metal discs
clues.BEAT: Regular pulse you can count while music plays
clues.HAND: Body part that holds and shakes the instrument
clues.TAP: Strike lightly with your fingers to make a beat

notes.JINGLE: The little metal discs strike one another when the tambourine moves. Several quick touches can make one bright ringing sound.

stairs-and-hallway-3.solvingTip: Start with the soft container for purchases. Then think about the band you lift and the curved support you hang it on.

clues.LOAD: Weight the filled shopping bag puts on the hook
clues.WALL: Upright surface the hook is fastened to

notes.HOOK: The strap hangs over the curve of the hook. The screw is the separate piece that holds the hook to the wall.

everyday-kitchen-repairs-3.solvingTip: Start with the short clue that means droop in the middle. Its crossings can help with the name for the piece underneath the shelf.

clues.BRACKET: Piece fixed under a shelf to hold it up
clues.LOAD: Weight the stack of dishes puts on the shelf
clues.SUPPORT: Hold up the weight of the plates and bowls

notes.SAG: A shelf can be firm at both ends and have its middle bend downward. That bend is what the short clue describes.
notes.SUPPORT: Support is the action of bearing the weight. The bracket is the piece underneath the shelf that does it.

fall-harvest-work-4.solvingTip: Look first for the tool that tells the clerk how heavy the pumpkin is. Then find the word for the units shown on it.

clues.PLATFORM: Flat part of the scale the pumpkin sits on
clues.STAND: Roadside place where shoppers can buy pumpkins
clues.LOAD: Weight resting on the scale's flat surface
clues.STEM: Short plant stalk still attached to the pumpkin

notes.SCALE: The pumpkin rests on the flat platform while the scale shows its weight. The pounds are the units on that reading.

drinks-poured-and-served-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for what comes out of the cold bin. Then find the tool that holds several pieces as you lift them.

clues.POUR: Tip the scoop so the ice falls into the pitcher
clues.CUBE: Block of ice with six square faces
clues.LOAD: Amount of ice carried in one scoop

notes.SCOOP: Here the word names the utensil. Its long handle reaches into the bin and its rounded end holds several pieces of ice.

optional-scenes-in-acts-and-joshua-5.solvingTip: Try the clue for the animals in the net. Then look for the plural word for what carried the fishers in Luke's story.

clues.LOAD: Weight of the fish the boats have to carry

notes.CATCH: Catch is a noun here. It means all the fish taken on this trip, which is why the fishers need help from another boat.

water-close-by-5.solvingTip: Look for the clue about the small flat rock first. Then find the two actions that take it across the water and below it.

clues.SINK: Go below the water when the bouncing stops
clues.RING: A circle that widens from the spot where the stone hits

notes.SKIP: The stone travels along the pond in several short bounces. Each touch can leave a circle spreading over the surface.

birds-to-recognize.solvingTip: Start with the hard mouthpart that taps the trunk. Its letters can help you name the outer part of the tree that the bird taps.

clues.CLAW: Curved nail the bird uses to grip the trunk
clues.FEATHER: One stiff part of a woodpecker's tail
clues.INSECT: Six-legged animal a woodpecker may find under bark

notes.BARK: The bird's feet grip the bark, the outer covering of the trunk. The wood lies underneath.
notes.FEATHER: A woodpecker can brace its stiff tail feathers against a trunk. Those feathers help support the bird as its feet grip the bark.
notes.INSECT: Some insects or their young live under bark. A woodpecker can peck at the trunk to reach them with its beak or tongue.

night-outdoors-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the bird first. Then look for the word that names the call you might hear from the roof.

clues.HUNT: Look for an animal to catch for food
clues.CLAW: One of the curved nails on an owl's foot
clues.FEATHER: One of the soft-edged parts on an owl's wing

notes.NIGHT: An owl's call can carry through a quiet barnyard after sunset. Dusk is the time when the last daylight fades.
notes.FEATHER: Many owls have soft edges on their flight feathers. Those edges help quiet the sound when the wings move.

kitchen-windowsill-greens-4.solvingTip: Look for the clue about the leaves you can reach first from the edge of the box. Then look for the middle, where the little leaves are growing.

clues.TENDER: Soft and easy to bite, like a young lettuce leaf

notes.OUTER: The outer leaves are the ones farthest from the middle of the plant. Smaller leaves can keep growing in the center.

before-the-first-bite-2.solvingTip: Try the plural clue for the two tools with points. Their letters can help with the action of pulling the chicken into thin pieces.

clues.TENDER: Easy to pull apart, as well-cooked chicken can be

notes.FORKS: One fork holds the chicken still while the other draws away a few strands. Their points do different jobs in the same motion.

welcoming-a-new-neighbor-2.solvingTip: Start with the short message left on the refrigerator. Then look for the word that tells what happens to the trash at the roadside.

clues.PICKUP: Scheduled collection of trash from the curb
clues.CURB: Raised street edge where residents set their trash bins

notes.CURB: The curb marks the edge of the street. That is where the collection truck can reach the bins.

breakfast-on-the-griddle.solvingTip: Start with the word for the browned bread. The longer clue names the narrow pieces cut from it.

clues.PICKUP: Act of lifting a strip of toast from the plate by hand

notes.STRIPS: Cutting from one end of the slice to the other makes longer pieces. Each narrow piece can be lifted separately.

optional-scenes-in-acts-and-joshua.solvingTip: Start with the structure the people walk around. Then use the longer clue for their instruments and the number from the final day in Joshua 6.

clues.SEVEN: How many times the people circle Jericho on the final day in Joshua 6
clues.STEPS: Movements made one at a time while walking
clues.LINE: Row of people walking one behind the next

notes.CIRCLE: The word describes going all the way around the city. Joshua 6 draws a distinction between one circuit on earlier days and seven on the final day.

autumn-kitchen-and-pantry-4.solvingTip: Start with the glass container on the shelf. Then look for the fruit named in the thick topping for toast.

clues.SPREAD: Soft topping you can smooth onto toast
clues.BUTTER: Second word in the name of a thick cooked apple spread
clues.SPOON: Utensil for taking some of the apple mixture from the jar
clues.THICK: Dense enough to stay on a spoon when lifted
clues.FRUIT: Kind of food cooked down to make apple butter
clues.SUGAR: Sweetener found naturally in apples or added to their spread

notes.BUTTER: Apple butter gets its name from its smooth texture. Apples cook down to a thick mixture that spreads easily on toast.
notes.FRUIT: Cooking the fruit slowly lets the apples soften and lets moisture escape. The thick spread gets much of its body from the apples themselves.
notes.SUGAR: Apples bring some sugar of their own to apple butter. As moisture cooks away, their flavor becomes stronger in the thick spread.

lunches-with-a-spoon-4.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the flat bread you dip or spread hummus on. Its letters can help with the longer word for the bean.

clues.SPREAD: Use a spoon to put an even layer of hummus on pita

notes.CHICKPEA: A chickpea is also called a garbanzo bean. Blending the beans gives the bowl of hummus its smooth base.

pantry-choices.solvingTip: Look for the clue for the part you twist off the jar. Then compare the two texture words printed on different peanut butter jars.

clues.BUTTER: Second word on a jar of ground peanuts
clues.SPREAD: Put an even layer of the topping on a slice of toast

kitchen-sandwich-sides-4.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the cooking liquid. Then look for the small dark fruits that get chopped into the topping.

clues.SPREAD: Put a thin layer of the olive topping on bread
clues.PASTE: Thick mixture of chopped olives and oil
clues.CRISP: Firm enough to snap, like the dry toast under the olives

notes.PASTE: Finely chopped olives and oil form a thick mixture that clings to the spoon. The puzzle uses the word for that texture.

kitchen-jars-and-tins.solvingTip: Look for the color of the strips first. Then use the crossings to name the pepper cut into those strips.

clues.SPREAD: Soft cheese mixture that can be smoothed onto a cracker

notes.PIMENTO: Chopped pimentos leave little red pieces in the cheese. They are a mild pepper you may recognize from the center of a stuffed olive.

gift-paper-folds.solvingTip: Try the three-letter clue for the object waved to move air. Then look for the narrow fold that lets it close neatly.

clues.SPREAD: Open the folded paper wide to show its shape

notes.PLEAT: Each pleat is a narrow fold. A row of folds lets the top open out while the base stays together.

keeping-winter-wet-out-2.solvingTip: Find the short clue for what moves around the drying mitten. Then try the clue for the frame that holds it up.

clues.SPREAD: Lay the mitten out so it lies open on the rack
clues.DRIP: A small drop falling from wet clothing

notes.DAMP: A damp mitten still holds a little water. Laying it open lets air reach more of the fabric while that water dries.

watching-small-changes-2.solvingTip: Start with the seasoning that stays on the plate. The other clues explain what the water does before those grains are visible.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward across the plate, as a thin puddle does
clues.TRACE: Very small amount left behind after most of something is gone

notes.GRAINS: As the water evaporates, the dissolved salt stays behind and can form little crystals. Their light color shows up against the plate.

listening-and-looking-outdoors-3.solvingTip: Try the clue for the insect's long supports first. Then look for the little dents those parts make in the water.

clues.SPREAD: Move outward, as a small wave does on the pond

notes.DIMPLES: A dimple is a dip in the surface. A ripple is a small wave that moves across it.

garden-birds-and-insects-3.solvingTip: Start with the short clue for the space between two points. Then look for the word for a single thread crossing that space.

clues.SPREAD: Extend outward as the web gets wider
clues.SILK: Strong fine material a spider makes for its web

notes.ANCHOR: An anchor is a place where a strand is held fast. A leaf or twig can give the spider a fixed point for starting a new thread.

small-habits-of-wild-neighbors-4.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter animal clue. Then find the word for its resting place and the action it takes when it opens its wings.

clues.SPREAD: Open the wings wide as the bat starts to fly
clues.HOLD: Keep the feet in place on the perch
clues.GRIP: Firm grasp the bat releases before it drops

notes.ROOST: A roost is where a bird or bat settles to rest. In this scene the bat lets go of its shelter at dusk.

sauces-and-table-spreads-5.solvingTip: Find the kitchen tool that is warmed first. Then look for the clue that describes the texture of what it will lift.

clues.PORTION: Amount of food set aside for one serving
clues.SPREAD: Soft topping that can be put on bread or crackers

notes.FIRM: The mixture is stiff enough to hold its shape. A spoon can take out one portion while the rest stays in the bowl.

snacks-for-a-table-3.solvingTip: Start with the clue for the round fruit. Then look for the action that moves one cut piece into the peanut butter.

clues.SPREAD: Soft topping such as peanut butter
clues.SLICE: One flat piece cut from the apple
clues.DIP: Put an apple piece briefly into the peanut butter

notes.APPLE: The core holds the seeds. You can cut pieces from around the core and dip the cut edges into the peanut butter.
notes.PLATE: A plate lets you set the apple slices out in a layer instead of a pile. Put the spread beside them so each slice can be dipped.
notes.KNIFE: Cut down beside the apple's core so the seeds stay in the middle piece. The knife can then divide the larger pieces into smaller slices for dipping.

community-volunteers-5.solvingTip: Start with the three-letter clue for what you drink from. Then look for the larger container where the coffee is kept.

clues.HALL: Large room where the church group meets
clues.TAP: Small spout that lets coffee out of the urn
clues.SUGAR: Sweetener set out for guests to stir into coffee

notes.HANDLE: A handle lets you carry or steady the container. The coffee comes out of the little tap at the bottom.
notes.SUGAR: At the coffee table, sugar can be set beside the cups. Each guest can add as much as they like after drawing coffee from the urn.

eating-at-the-diner-2.solvingTip: Try the short clue for the bread first. Then look for what the bees make to sweeten the open halves.

clues.BUTTER: Cream-based topping that melts on warm bread
clues.SPREAD: Smooth an even layer of the topping over a cut half

notes.HONEY: Honey flows slowly. Tiny openings in the soft inside of the roll let a little of it soak in.

garden-small-spaces-2.solvingTip: Try the drink at 10 Across, which you can make with a few mint sprigs. One crossing helps name the green part at 6 Down.

notes.GLASS: The glass is the cup for the finished drink. A mint sprig can rest on top of the ice, where you can smell the leaves as you take a sip.

clues.GLASS: Drinking vessel for iced tea with a sprig of mint

garden-small-spaces-3.solvingTip: Begin with the short cutting action at 5 Down. Its crossing helps name the bulb at 6 Across whose flavor chives bring to a dish.

clues.STEM: Thin stalk that holds up a chive flower
clues.SCISSORS: Two-bladed tool for snipping chive leaves
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable with a flavor similar to chives

notes.WATER: In a patio pot, the roots take up water from the soil. The narrow green leaves above the soil are the part you cut for a topping.
notes.SCISSORS: Kitchen scissors make it easy to snip a few chive leaves above the soil. You can also use them to cut the long leaves into short pieces for soup.
notes.ONION: Chives and onions are close relatives, which helps explain their similar flavor. In this scene the snipped green leaves give the dish a mild onion taste.

garden-small-spaces-4.solvingTip: Picture what holds the basket up at 8 Down. The crossing at 8 Across asks what you do when you put the basket on that support.

clues.BERRY: Small juicy fruit such as a strawberry
clues.FRUIT: General name for produce such as apples and strawberries
clues.FLOWER: Blossom that comes before a strawberry

notes.WATER: A hanging basket can dry out more quickly than a garden bed. Water goes into the soil in the basket, where the strawberry roots can take it up.
notes.SWEET: Ripe strawberries can taste sweet without any added sugar. Look below the basket's rim as well as over the leaves, since fruit can hang on either side.
notes.FLOWER: The strawberry blossom comes before the ripe berry. After pollination, the middle of the blossom can grow into the red part you eat.

garden-small-spaces-5.solvingTip: Start with what shines on the deck at 2 Down. Then try its crossing at 4 Across, a word for something you could make with the ripe pepper.

notes.SWEET: Sweet describes a kind of pepper with little or no heat. A green sweet pepper often tastes less sugary than the same kind allowed to ripen to red.
notes.GREEN: Many sweet peppers start out green and can change color as they ripen. On some varieties, red is the color they take on later.

clues.SWEET: Mild in flavor, as a pepper without a hot bite
clues.GREEN: Color a sweet pepper often has before it turns red

garden-evening-chores.solvingTip: Find where you stop the water at 1 Across. It shares a square with the twisting action at 1 Down.

clues.REEL: Spool you wind the garden hose around

notes.REEL: A hose reel holds the tubing in a circle. You can turn it to bring the hose in a little at a time.
notes.WATER: After the tap is turned off, some water can stay in the hose. Lifting one end can help that last bit drain before you wind the hose onto its reel.

garden-evening-chores-3.solvingTip: Try the center of the apple at 10 Down. Its crossing at 9 Across asks for a harvesting action.

notes.SWEET: Ripe fallen apples can vary in sweetness. An apple that tastes sweet by itself can still add a little tartness to a batch of pressed cider.
notes.JUICE: Freshly pressed apple juice can darken as it stands in the air. Color can also vary with the apples that went into the press.
notes.APPLE: An apple that drops from a tree on its own is a windfall. It can have a bruise where it hit the ground even if the peel stays intact.

clues.JUICE: Liquid that comes out when apples are pressed
clues.APPLE: Round fruit that may be gathered after it drops from a tree

garden-evening-chores-4.solvingTip: Start with what you write on an envelope to remember when you saved the seeds at 6 Across. The crossing at 5 Down names what the envelope is made of.

notes.PAPER: A paper envelope can hold seeds once they are dry. Write the plant name and date on the outside so you can tell it from other saved seed.
notes.SEED: The dry seed is what can grow next season. Let the marigold heads dry so the seeds come out more easily before you fill and label the envelope.
notes.ENVELOPE: A closed paper envelope keeps the tiny seeds together. Fold the flap down firmly so the seeds stay inside when the envelope is moved.

clues.PAPER: Material used to make envelopes for saved seeds
clues.ENVELOPE: Folded paper holder you can use to store dried seeds

garden-evening-chores-5.solvingTip: Picture the patch of soil that gets a layer of mulch at 3 Down. It crosses the little unwanted plant at 4 Across.

clues.LOAD: Amount of mulch the wheelbarrow is carrying
clues.HANDLE: One of the two grips used to push a wheelbarrow
clues.WHEEL: Round part at the front of a wheelbarrow that rolls on the path

notes.HANDLE: A wheelbarrow usually has two long handles, one for each hand. Lifting them shifts the load onto the front wheel so it can roll.
notes.WHEEL: One front wheel carries much of the load in a typical wheelbarrow. As it rolls, the two handles let you guide the wheel along the path and steady the load.

garden-from-the-beginning.solvingTip: Look at 1 Across for a line of seedlings. Its crossing at 1 Down names the part growing down into the soil.

clues.MIST: Spray a light cloud of water over the seedlings
clues.NAME: Word on a marker that tells which plant is growing
clues.LIGHT: Brightness that helps seedlings grow above the soil
clues.PENCIL: Writing tool for marking a wooden plant tag

notes.LABEL: The label is the marker itself. The word on it tells you which plant is growing in that spot.
notes.LIGHT: Light reaches the seedlings above the soil. The markers can face the front of the tray so you can read the names without moving the young plants.
notes.PENCIL: A pencil can leave a readable mark on some plant tags made of unfinished wood. Write the name and date before pushing the tag into the tray.

garden-from-the-beginning-2.solvingTip: Find the glass container at 7 Down. Then try the crossing at 9 Across for how the paper feels when it is a little wet.

clues.WATCH: Look closely as the first root appears
clues.GLASS: Clear material that lets you watch a seed grow in a jar
clues.PAPER: Sheet material kept damp beside a bean as it sprouts

notes.WATCH: Watch is an action here. The clear jar lets you see the little root grow without moving the bean.
notes.GLASS: The glass wall lets you watch a root develop without digging up the bean. A damp paper lining can hold the seed where you can see it.
notes.PAPER: Damp paper holds the bean against the side of the jar without covering it with soil. That leaves the root visible as it starts to grow.

garden-from-the-beginning-4.solvingTip: Try the long-handled garden tool at 1 Down. It crosses the straight mark or guide at 2 Across.

clues.LINE: Straight mark or guide for spacing the onions
clues.SKIN: Thin papery covering on the outside of an onion
clues.BULB: Round part of an onion made of layers
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable grown from sets in a garden row

notes.WHITE: White and red describe common kinds of onion. The dry outer layer of a white onion is pale, and the fleshy layers inside can look almost clear when sliced thin.
notes.ONION: Small onion bulbs planted in spring are often called sets. Each can grow into a larger onion if there is room between the plants in the row.

garden-from-the-beginning-5.solvingTip: Begin with the tool at 6 Down that cuts the young squash from its stem. Use a crossing for the longer squash name at 8 Across.

clues.SKIN: Outside covering of the young squash
clues.STEM: Stalk that holds the squash on the plant
clues.SUMMER: Warm season when young zucchini is often picked
clues.KNIFE: Bladed tool for cutting a young squash from the vine

notes.BASKET: A young zucchini has tender skin that can bruise. A shallow basket lets you carry the squash without piling heavier produce on top.
notes.SUMMER: Zucchini is often picked in summer before the squash reaches its full size. At that stage the skin is tender enough to leave on for cooking.
notes.KNIFE: A garden knife can cut through the firm stem above a young zucchini. That lets the squash come free without pulling the vine along with it.

garden-welcoming-corners.solvingTip: Find the edge of the shallow bowl at 3 Down. It shares a square with the bird with the orange-red breast at 3 Across.

notes.WATER: A shallow layer of water gives a small bird a place to stand while it splashes. The raised rim is another place for birds to perch.
notes.FEATHER: After splashing in a birdbath, a bird may shake water from its feathers. It can use its beak to arrange them again as they dry.

garden-welcoming-corners-2.solvingTip: Begin with the long seat at 9 Across. Then try the crossing for the part of the shrub that hangs above it at 5 Down.

notes.BRANCH: Lilac flower clusters grow near the ends of woody stems. A branch reaches out over the bench, holding the blooms above the seat.

clues.BRANCH: Woody part of a lilac that reaches out above a bench

garden-welcoming-corners-3.solvingTip: Start with the bright object that makes a shadow at 9 Across. A crossing leads to what holds the sundial up at 7 Down.

notes.LIGHT: Sunlight striking the raised part of the sundial casts a shadow across the face. As the shadow moves, it points to different hour marks.

clues.LIGHT: What the sun provides so a sundial can cast a shadow

garden-welcoming-corners-4.solvingTip: Look at 7 Down for the time when daylight begins to fade. The crossing at 11 Across asks what softens the lantern's glare.

clues.SHADE: Cover around the lantern's light that softens its glare
clues.HANDLE: Loop you hold to carry a lantern

notes.SHADE: A lantern shade can shield your eyes from the brightest part and send more light toward the path.
notes.HANDLE: The loop at the top of a lantern can serve two jobs. You can carry the lantern by it or slip it over a hook.
notes.LIGHT: A hanging lantern casts light down onto the path. At dusk, the glow can help show where the edge of the walk is.

garden-welcoming-corners-5.solvingTip: Try the footwear that keeps mud off your foot at 5 Across. Its crossing names the walking route through the beds at 2 Down.

clues.STONE: Hard piece of rock set into the garden path
clues.MUD: Wet soil a boot can pick up beside the stones

notes.STONE: Set underfoot, a broad stone gives you a firm spot to step. It keeps your boot above the softer soil beside it.

garden-keeping-tools.solvingTip: Picture the curved support on the shed wall at 2 Across. The crossing at 2 Down asks for the part of a tool you hold.

clues.FORK: Garden tool with points for loosening soil

notes.FORK: The long points of a garden fork loosen packed earth. Pressing down on the top helps those points go into the soil.
notes.HANDLE: A trowel has a short handle so you can work close to the soil. Some handles have a hole at the end, which lets the tool hang on a hook.

garden-keeping-tools-2.solvingTip: Begin with the part of the fence that swings open at 7 Down. It crosses the action you take to shut it at 11 Across.

notes.HANDLE: The handle gives you a grip for pulling the gate shut. The latch is the separate part that catches and holds the gate there.
notes.PAINT: A fresh coat of paint can cover exposed wood after a gate is repaired. The hinge still needs room to move as the paint dries.
notes.FENCE: The fence stays in place as the gate swings on its hinges. If the gate sags, the post may need to be checked as well as the hinge.

clues.HANDLE: Part you pull to close a garden gate
clues.PAINT: Liquid coating that can cover bare wood on a repaired gate

garden-keeping-tools-3.solvingTip: Start with the part that covers the barrel at 7 Down. Then use a crossing to find what water does when it runs out at 9 Across.

garden-keeping-tools-4.solvingTip: Try the inside surface of your hand at 10 Across. The crossing at 6 Down is what you do when you hold a tool securely.

clues.COTTON: Plant fiber sometimes used for a garden glove's back or cuff

garden-keeping-tools-5.solvingTip: Find the short action at 3 Down for what the shears do. Its crossing at 4 Across names one woody plant in the hedge.

clues.LEVEL: Flat and even in height along the top
clues.TRIM: Make the whole hedge neat by cutting along its top
clues.CLIP: Snip off a single leaf or twig with one quick motion
clues.BRANCH: Woody part of a hedge that can be trimmed back

notes.LEVEL: Level describes the result along the top. You can compare the height at both ends to see whether one side is higher.
notes.BRANCH: A branch has older woody growth under its leaves. Shears trim the smaller tips to even out the hedge, while a bigger branch may need a different tool.
notes.GREEN: The hedge looks green where the leafy shoots cover its branches. A deep cut into old wood can expose bare areas under that outer layer.

garden-fruit-trees.solvingTip: Look first for the fruit at 6 Down that is wider at the bottom. It shares a square with the seed-bearing center at 9 Across.

clues.STEM: Short stalk attaching the pear to the branch
clues.YELLOW: Ripe-lemon color that can appear on pear skin

notes.YELLOW: Some pear varieties change from green to yellow as they ripen. The skin color is only one sign, since other varieties can stay green when ripe.
notes.BASKET: Set the pears in the basket gently as you pick them. A shallow layer helps keep the fruit underneath from being pressed by the rest.
notes.BRANCH: A pear hangs from a short fruit stem attached to the branch or a smaller offshoot. The stem can come away with the fruit while the branch stays on the tree.

garden-fruit-trees-2.solvingTip: Find the hard piece in the middle of a peach at 7 Across. The crossing at 6 Down describes when the fruit is ready to pick.

notes.SLICE: Peach slices can be cut away from the pit one at a time. A soft ripe peach is easier to slice without pressing hard on the skin.
notes.FRUIT: The peach is a fruit with a single hard pit. Fuzzy skin and soft flesh can help you recognize it before the pit is visible.

clues.FRUIT: Food group that includes peaches and plums

garden-fruit-trees-3.solvingTip: Start with the dish that holds the washed plums at 5 Across. Follow its crossing at 2 Down to the flavor that reminds you of sugar.

clues.PICK: Gather ripe plums from the branches
clues.PIT: Hard center stone removed from a plum

notes.PICK: Pick names the action of taking a plum off its branch. The fruit still has its hard center when you carry it inside.
notes.SWEET: A ripe plum can have sweet flesh next to a rather tart skin. You may notice both tastes in the same bite.
notes.FRUIT: A plum is a stone fruit, so its juicy flesh surrounds one hard pit. That is also why a plum can be cut into pieces that lift away from the center.

garden-fruit-trees-4.solvingTip: Think of a baked dessert with a cherry filling at 10 Across. At 10 Down, the crossing asks for the hard center you take out before baking.

clues.STEM: Thin stalk that attaches a cherry to the branch
clues.JUICE: Liquid released when a cherry is cut or crushed

notes.BASKET: Use a small basket for cherries so the top layer stays within reach. Some cherries may come off the branch with their paired stems still joined.
notes.JUICE: A ripe cherry can release red juice when you cut it or remove its pit. The liquid is what can leave a colored spot on the cutting board.

garden-fruit-trees-5.solvingTip: Try the sharp taste at 10 Across. Use one of its letters to help with the yellow citrus fruit at 5 Down.

clues.JUICE: Liquid squeezed from the flesh of a lemon
clues.WHEEL: Rolling part under a plant tub that helps it move

notes.JUICE: Squeezing the lemon releases liquid from its flesh. The rind is the outside layer and can be used separately.
notes.WHEEL: A wheel under the tub can take part of the weight of the soil. With the tub on a wheeled stand, you can move the tree toward a sunnier spot.

animals-on-the-farm.solvingTip: Start with the adult bird leading the young chicks at 2 Down. The crossing at 5 Across asks what a chick hatches from.

notes.FEATHER: A chick's first covering is usually soft down. As it grows, longer feathers appear, including the ones along the wings.

animals-on-the-farm-3.solvingTip: Find what covers the lamb and can be spun into yarn at 7 Down. It crosses the color clue at 7 Across.

notes.GRASS: Grass is what the ewes can graze on while the lamb rests nearby. The pasture is the whole area where the flock feeds and stays together.

clues.GRASS: Narrow-leaved plants that sheep can graze on

animals-on-the-farm-4.solvingTip: Look for the short name for a young goat at 9 Down. Use a crossing for the hair on the adult goat's chin at 10 Across.

notes.FENCE: A goat may raise its front feet onto a sturdy part of the fence to see over it. If the fence has horizontal rails, spaces between them also give it a view through to the hay.
notes.TAIL: A goat usually carries its short tail raised. The long hair under its chin is the beard, a feature you can see from across the fence.

clues.FENCE: Barrier with posts that a goat might look over

animals-on-the-farm-5.solvingTip: Try the body part used for hearing at 5 Across. Its crossing helps with the name at 2 Down for an animal with a donkey father and a horse mother.

small-wild-visitors.solvingTip: Begin with how a rabbit moves in one short jump at 9 Down. Then look at the crossing for the part it uses to sniff at 10 Across.

notes.GRASS: A rabbit can feed on grass near a blackberry bush and move under the branches for cover. The bush and the low growth underneath give it different places to hide.

clues.GRASS: Low green growth a rabbit may eat beside a bush

small-wild-visitors-2.solvingTip: Start with the hard-shelled food a chipmunk might carry at 4 Across. The crossing at 5 Down names the part behind its body.

clues.PAW: Foot a chipmunk uses to hold a seed
clues.SEED: Small plant part a chipmunk may carry in its cheek pouch

notes.SEED: A chipmunk can tuck several seeds into its cheek pouches. The pouches help it carry the seeds away from the step in one trip.

small-wild-visitors-3.solvingTip: Try the covering that the raccoon's dark eye markings resemble at 10 Across. Its crossing at 6 Down names the small stream beside it.

clues.MASK: Face covering the raccoon's dark eye markings resemble
clues.RING: Band of color around the raccoon's tail
clues.WATER: Liquid flowing in the creek beside the raccoon

notes.WATER: The water in the creek follows its channel. The bank is the ground at either side where the raccoon can walk.
notes.NIGHT: Raccoons often become active after dark. At night a raccoon can move along the creek bank looking for food.

small-wild-visitors-4.solvingTip: Find the face part you use to notice a smell at 8 Down. Then look across at 7 Across for the striped animal crossing the yard.

clues.TAIL: Part behind the skunk's body that it can lift

notes.WHITE: A striped skunk's white markings stand out against its black fur. The stripes can vary in width and may extend onto the tail.
notes.NIGHT: A skunk often comes out at night to look for food. In dim light, the pale stripes can stand out more than the darker fur around them.
notes.GRASS: Short yard grass leaves the skunk's dark body and pale stripes easier to see. Taller grass along the edge of a yard can hide most of its body.

small-wild-visitors-5.solvingTip: Begin with the place a mother carries her young at 8 Down. Its crossing at 9 Across can help you spell the name of this nighttime animal.

clues.POUCH: Pocket on a mother opossum's belly that holds her young
clues.TAIL: Long part behind the opossum's body
clues.PAW: Foot the opossum uses to grip a branch

notes.TAIL: An opossum's mostly bare tail can help it keep its balance. The animal also grips branches with its feet.
notes.NIGHT: An opossum that rests in a sheltered place by day may climb after dark. In this scene, its paws help it hold onto the branch at night.
notes.TREE: A tree can give an opossum a place to climb away from the ground. Smaller branches connected to the trunk can serve as routes across the tree.

birds-to-recognize-2.solvingTip: Try the color clue at 2 Across for the shade of a clear sky. It crosses the part of the oak where the bird can land at 2 Down.

notes.WHITE: A blue jay has pale or white underparts. White markings on the wings and tail can also stand out against the darker blue feathers.
notes.BRANCH: A blue jay can grip an oak branch while it looks around. The acorn is part of the oak's crop, and the branch gives the bird a place to pause.
notes.FEATHER: Tiny structures inside a blue jay's feathers scatter light in a way that looks blue to us. The white markings sit beside that blue on parts of its wings and tail.

birds-to-recognize-3.solvingTip: Look for the tiny part of a plant that the birds pick up at 8 Down. Its crossing at 9 Across asks for the action of settling on a stem.

clues.PERCH: Settle on a stem or branch
clues.YELLOW: Bright feather color of a male goldfinch in spring

notes.YELLOW: A male American goldfinch often has bright yellow feathers and dark wings in spring and summer. Its plumage can look duller in winter.

birds-to-recognize-4.solvingTip: Find the short action for taking a little drink at 3 Across. Then look at the crossing for the part that keeps the bird in the air at 1 Down.

clues.SUGAR: Sweet ingredient often added to water for a bird feeder

notes.SUGAR: Flower nectar already contains sugar. In this garden scene it is the sweetness that draws the bird to the blossoms.
notes.WATER: Plain water dissolves sugar in a hummingbird feeder. The flowers in the same scene make their own sweet liquid, called nectar.
notes.FLOWER: The red flower is a source of nectar for the hummingbird. A feeder nearby can hold a separate sugar-and-water mixture.

birds-to-recognize-5.solvingTip: Start with the shape of the turkey's spread-out tail at 1 Down. The crossing at 4 Across asks for another feathered part used in flight.

notes.SEED: A wild turkey can pick up seeds as it walks along the edge of the woods. It may scratch among fallen leaves to uncover them.

beside-the-water.solvingTip: Try the barrier the beaver can build across the stream at 3 Across. At 2 Down, its crossing leads to the word for the beaver's home.

notes.TREE: A beaver can gnaw through the base of a small tree with its front teeth. It can use branches from the fallen tree as material for a dam or lodge.
notes.TAIL: A beaver swims with its broad tail helping it steer. It can slap the water with that tail when it is alarmed.

clues.TREE: Plant with a woody trunk that a beaver can gnaw through

beside-the-water-2.solvingTip: Find the familiar word for moving through the river at 1 Across. Its crossing at 2 Down asks what the otter moves through.

clues.WATER: Liquid in the river where the otter swims

notes.WATER: The otter can slide into the water and swim after a fish. On the bank its paws help it travel over land.

beside-the-water-3.solvingTip: Start at 5 Down with the action that takes the bird headfirst into the water. It crosses the long bird name at 6 Across.

notes.WATER: From a branch over the pond, a kingfisher can look down through the water for a fish. Its splash comes when it dives.
notes.BRANCH: The branch above the pond is the kingfisher's perch. From there the bird can watch for movement in the water before leaving the branch to dive.

clues.WATER: Liquid a kingfisher dives into for a fish
clues.BRANCH: Tree limb a kingfisher can perch on above a pond

beside-the-water-4.solvingTip: Find the short word for the tall bird's walking limb at 6 Down. Then try the crossing about how deep the water is at 4 Across.

notes.WATER: A heron can stand in shallow water with its body held well above the surface. Its legs let it look down for fish without having to swim.

beside-the-water-5.solvingTip: Look for the broad floating leaf at 1 Down. Its crossing at 3 Across names the still body of water that holds it.

clues.HOVER: Stay in one spot in the air above the pond
clues.WING: One of four thin parts a dragonfly uses to fly
clues.PAD: Broad floating leaf of a water lily
clues.WATER: Liquid a lily pad floats on
clues.INSECT: Kind of six-legged animal that includes a dragonfly
clues.STEM: Plant stalk that can reach from below the pond's surface

notes.WATER: Dragonflies often fly over water because their young develop below the surface. The adults in this scene hover above the lily pads.
notes.INSECT: A dragonfly is an insect with two pairs of wings. It can hover over a pond and then change direction quickly to catch smaller insects.
notes.STEM: A water lily's flower grows on a stalk that reaches toward the surface. The floating pad is a leaf with a long stalk of its own.

looking-at-the-shore-3.solvingTip: Find the short word for the salt water beyond the rocks at 1 Across. Its crossing at 1 Down helps you name the animal resting there.

notes.WATER: The seals can dive into the water for fish and come back onto the rock to rest. Their flippers help them move between the two places.

clues.WATER: Liquid a seal swims through to catch fish

looking-at-the-shore-4.solvingTip: Look at 1 Down for the hard mouthpart above the pelican's pouch. It shares a letter with the liquid below the bird at 3 Across.

clues.POUCH: Stretchy pocket below a pelican's bill
clues.WATER: What a pelican drains from its bill after catching fish

notes.WHITE: An American white pelican has a mostly white body and dark wing tips that are especially easy to see in flight. The pouch is beneath the bill.
notes.WATER: A pelican's pouch can take in water with a catch of fish. It can drain the water from its bill before swallowing the fish.

looking-at-the-shore-5.solvingTip: Start with the shore grains under the bird's feet at 5 Across. Its crossing helps you spell the long shorebird name at 1 Down.

trees-and-their-fruit.solvingTip: Find the flat part that makes a maple seed spin at 1 Across. A crossing leads to the place where the seed lands at 2 Down.

clues.FALL: Move down from the branch to the ground
clues.SEED: Small part inside a maple's winged fruit that can grow into a tree

notes.BRANCH: The maple branch supports a cluster of seeds while they develop. After they come loose, their papery wings help them spin as they fall.
notes.SEED: The seed sits in a small pouch at the base of the maple's papery wing. The wing helps it spin away from the branch as it falls.
notes.SHADE: A maple's leaves cast shade underneath the branches. A falling seed can spin through that shaded space before it reaches the ground.

trees-and-their-fruit-2.solvingTip: Start with the short word for the food that has a hard shell at 1 Across. The crossing at 2 Down tells you what it grows on.

clues.NUT: Edible part inside a walnut's hard shell
clues.SHADE: Cool area under the walnut tree, out of direct sun

notes.BRANCH: A walnut develops on a branch before it is picked or falls. On the table, you can crack its shell to reach the edible kernel.
notes.SHADE: Shade from the walnut tree can reach the picnic table. The leaves reduce the direct sun where people are sitting, leaving the light softer over the table.
notes.SHELL: A walnut shell has a line where its two halves meet. Cracking along that line can help you lift out a larger piece of the kernel.

trees-and-their-fruit-3.solvingTip: Look at 9 Down for what a flexible branch does when it curves downward. It crosses the land along the creek at 9 Across.

clues.BEND: Curve as a long willow branch does over the creek
clues.WATER: What flows under the willow branches

notes.WATER: The flexible branches of a willow can hang low over a creek. The water keeps flowing underneath even when the breeze moving the branches dies down.
notes.GREEN: The new willow leaves can give the branches a light green look in spring. Long clusters of those narrow leaves hang toward the creek.

trees-and-their-fruit-4.solvingTip: Try the covering on the outside of the trunk at 2 Across. A crossing helps start the name of the pale-barked tree at 2 Down.

clues.PEEL: Come away in a thin layer, as birch bark does
clues.PAPER: Writing material that thin birch bark can resemble

notes.BRANCH: A birch branch joins the trunk and carries leaves out toward the light. On birches with white bark, younger twigs near the tips can have a darker surface.
notes.PAPER: Thin layers of birch bark can peel back like sheets of paper. Here paper describes the bark's appearance. The pale layer is still part of the tree.
notes.SHADE: In a wooded spot, trunks can sit in shade while upper branches catch the sun. The pale bark of a birch can still be easy to pick out among darker trees.

trees-and-their-fruit-5.solvingTip: Start with the short word for what is inside the hard shell at 11 Across. Then try the crossing at 7 Down for how the prickly case opens.

clues.FALL: Drop from a tree, as a ripe nut does
clues.SHELL: Smooth brown covering of the nut inside its prickly case

notes.BRANCH: The chestnut grows inside a prickly case on the branch. As the case ripens and splits, the smooth nut can fall to the ground.
notes.TREE: A chestnut tree can have long leaves with toothed edges. Those edges give you something to look for even before the prickly cases open.
notes.SHELL: The prickly case around a chestnut opens as it ripens. Inside, each nut has its own smooth brown shell.

quiet-outdoor-moments.solvingTip: Look for the ripe-tomato color at 11 Down. It crosses a second rainbow color at 10 Across, the one you see in leaves.

notes.YELLOW: In a usual rainbow, yellow lies between orange and green. The curved band can be visible while rain is still falling farther away.
notes.GREEN: Green sits next to yellow on a rainbow's cooler side. The arc shows those color bands most clearly when you look toward a passing shower with the sun behind you.

clues.GREEN: Rainbow color next to yellow on its cooler side

quiet-outdoor-moments-2.solvingTip: Start with the early light that arrives before sunrise at 4 Down. Its crossing helps you spell the word for an image you can see on still water at 7 Across.

clues.SOFT: Gentle, like morning light through the mist

notes.SOFT: Mist can make the morning light look muted, the way a lamp looks through a thin curtain.

quiet-outdoor-moments-3.solvingTip: Find the word for one little bit of water at 2 Across. The crossing at 2 Down names the drops you see on the grass in the morning.

notes.LIGHT: At first light, tiny drops of dew can reflect the sun. That is what makes some drops sparkle while the grass around them still looks dark.
notes.GRASS: Drops of dew can sit along the narrow blades of grass. They may dry away first in the parts of the meadow that the morning sun reaches.
notes.STEM: Dew can gather at places where leaves meet the grass stem. That stem can also hold a seed head above the shorter blades.

clues.LIGHT: Brightness that makes drops of dew sparkle
clues.GRASS: Narrow-leaved growth that can hold dew on its blades
clues.STEM: Stalk on which blades of grass can grow

quiet-outdoor-moments-4.solvingTip: Try the word at 9 Across that tells how you can see the stones through the water. It crosses the clue for a small wave at 4 Down.

clues.SAND: Fine grains that can settle between brook pebbles

quiet-outdoor-moments-5.solvingTip: Start with the moving air at 9 Across, which you can hear in the grass. Its crossing names the open, grassy place at 6 Down.

clues.BEND: Curve toward the ground when the air moves
clues.GREEN: Common color of meadow grass in warm weather

notes.GREEN: A meadow can be green lower down while the tops of some stalks look tan. The lighter tips may carry the grass seeds.
notes.GRASS: The sound in the meadow can come from grass blades rubbing together. The taller stems bend a little with each passing breeze.

night-outdoors.solvingTip: Find the brief burst of light at 2 Across. The crossing at 1 Down asks for the verb meaning to shine with a softer light.

clues.WING: Thin part an insect uses to fly
clues.SUMMER: Warm season when fireflies often flash over a lawn
clues.INSECT: Kind of six-legged animal that includes fireflies

notes.SUMMER: On a summer evening, the flashes can become easier to see as the lawn darkens. Fireflies use the flashes as signals to other fireflies.
notes.GRASS: The grass gives the tiny flashes a darker background as evening falls. A firefly can lift off above the lawn, where the flash is easier to see.
notes.INSECT: A firefly is a kind of beetle. The glow comes from its body, and the wings let it carry that flash above the grass.

night-outdoors-4.solvingTip: Try the short name at 7 Across for the flying mammal. It crosses the time of day when the animal is active at 2 Down.

notes.NIGHT: Dusk is when daylight is fading. Bats that start hunting then can stay out at night, when they find insects even in the dark.
notes.INSECT: Some bats catch flying insects such as moths above a garden. A moth has six legs, while the bat has wings made from skin stretched along its forelimbs.

clues.NIGHT: Dark part of the day that follows dusk

night-outdoors-5.solvingTip: Look at 2 Down for the object that gives off light near the front door. Its crossing names the covered area where the moth rests at 5 Across.

clues.LAMP: Fixture that gives off light beside the front door
clues.WING: Broad part the moth uses to fly
clues.WINDOW: Opening with glass near the porch lamp
clues.SHADE: Cover that fits around a porch lamp
clues.INSECT: Kind of six-legged creature that includes moths

notes.WINDOW: The porch light can make the glass of the nearby window glow from the outside. A moth may rest on the frame or the siding beside it.
notes.SHADE: In this scene, shade means the cover around the porch lamp. It can direct the light downward, where a moth may be easier to notice.
notes.INSECT: A moth is an insect with wings covered in tiny scales. Those scales can look like fine dust when a few rub off.

breakfast-from-the-stove.solvingTip: Look at 9 Across for what you crack before whisking. One of its letters helps with the dairy spread that goes into the warm skillet at 7 Down.

notes.PLATE: The frying pan is where the eggs cook. The plate is where you put the finished scramble so it can go straight to the table.
notes.BUTTER: A little butter melted in the pan coats the surface for the eggs. The whisk is used earlier, while the eggs are still in the mixing bowl.

clues.BUTTER: Dairy fat often melted in a pan before eggs go in

breakfast-from-the-stove-2.solvingTip: Try the action that turns a pancake over at 6 Down. Its crossing helps you name the flat vessel it cooks in at 8 Across.

notes.PLATE: A flat plate gives the stack a steady base. It also catches syrup that runs down the sides when you cut into the pancakes.
notes.BUTTER: A pat of butter can soften on the top pancake. The syrup can then spread over the top and run down the sides of the stack.

clues.BUTTER: Cream-based spread that melts on warm pancakes

breakfast-from-the-stove-5.solvingTip: Start with the liquid cooking fat that keeps the grated potato from sticking at 8 Across. A crossing gives you a letter for the layered vegetable at 5 Down.

clues.BROWN: Cook until a darker crust forms on the potatoes
clues.PLATE: Flat dish you serve hash browns on
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable sometimes grated into hash browns
clues.POTATO: Starchy vegetable grated to make hash browns

notes.PLATE: Hash browns can be served on one side of a plate next to the eggs. The crisp outside is made in the pan before the potatoes are served.
notes.ONION: Grating onion with the potatoes spreads its flavor through the hash browns. Small pieces cook along with the potatoes as the outside crisps.
notes.POTATO: Grate the potato into thin shreds so they can brown together. Pressing out some of the moisture first helps the outside crisp in the pan.

bowls-of-soup.solvingTip: Find the deep vessel the soup cooks in at 1 Down. Its crossing points to the smaller round dish that gets carried to the table at 3 Across.

notes.SPOON: A soup spoon can hold broth and a few noodles at once. The deeper ladle moves a larger amount from the pot into the bowl.
notes.CARROT: Small carrot slices soften in chicken broth as the soup cooks. Their orange color makes them easy to pick out among the noodles.

clues.SPOON: Utensil that can hold a bite of noodles and broth
clues.CARROT: Orange root that can be sliced into chicken noodle soup

bowls-of-soup-2.solvingTip: Start at 9 Down with the color of a ripe tomato. A crossing leads to the crisp dry snack served with the soup at 8 Across.

notes.SPOON: A spoon can stir the tomato soup all the way down to the bottom of the pot. At the table, small spoonfuls give you a chance to let the hot soup cool.
notes.TOMATO: As tomatoes cook, their pieces soften enough to blend into a smooth soup. A few leaves of basil can add a fresh scent just before serving.

clues.TOMATO: Red fruit cooked until soft for a smooth soup

bowls-of-soup-3.solvingTip: Look for the small green vegetable that gives this dish its name at 10 Down. That word crosses the liquid dish it goes into at 9 Across.

clues.BONE: Hard part of a ham that can flavor the broth
clues.HAM: Cured pork simmered with the peas
clues.CARROT: Orange root vegetable sometimes diced into split pea soup

notes.WATER: Dried split peas absorb some of the water as they cook. As they soften and break apart, they help turn the cooking liquid into thick soup.
notes.SPOON: Split peas soften until the soup is thick enough to cling to the back of a spoon. A ladle is handy when you are filling an entire bowl.
notes.CARROT: Diced carrot can cook in the pot while the split peas soften. The pieces stay visible in the green soup even after the peas have broken down.

bowls-of-soup-4.solvingTip: Try the cooking vessel that holds the broth at 4 Across. Its crossing names the deep dish the broth is served in at 3 Down.

notes.CARROT: Cut the carrot into pieces about the same size so it softens evenly in the stock. Its small pieces can be ladled out with the beans and corn.

bowls-of-soup-5.solvingTip: Try the short temperature word at 9 Down. The crossing at 10 Across asks what heat does to the cheese.

notes.CHEESE: A slice of toast can float on the soup and support the grated cheese. As it melts, the cheese spreads over the toast and browns at the top.
notes.SPOON: The spoon can break through the softened toast and lift the onion broth underneath. A little melted cheese may come up in the same bite.

clues.CHEESE: Dairy topping that melts over toast in onion soup
clues.SPOON: Bowl-ended utensil used to eat onion soup

sandwich-counter.solvingTip: Start with what turns the sandwich to its other side at 6 Across. Then use one of its letters for the single piece cut from the bread at 4 Down.

clues.FLIP: Turn the sandwich over to cook the other side

notes.CHEESE: Cheese is the filling that softens between the bread slices. The butter goes on the outsides so the bread browns against the skillet.
notes.SLICE: The cheese can go on as a thin slice so it covers much of the bread. The bread slices hold that filling on either side as it melts.
notes.BUTTER: Butter the bread on the sides that will touch the skillet. Those surfaces crisp as the cheese softens between the slices.

sandwich-counter-2.solvingTip: Find the glass container at 2 Down. Its crossing at 2 Across names the fruit spread on one side of the sandwich.

notes.BREAD: Soft bread holds the two spreads together. Putting peanut butter on the bread first can help keep the jelly from soaking straight into the slice.
notes.CRUST: The crust is the baked edge around the soft middle of each bread slice. It can stay on a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, or be trimmed away after the sandwich is assembled.
notes.SANDWICH: Peanut butter and jelly can be spread on separate bread slices before they are brought together. The sandwich can then be cut across the middle for two smaller portions.

clues.BREAD: Baked food that holds the peanut butter and jelly
clues.CRUST: Outer baked edge of the bread in a sandwich

sandwich-counter-3.solvingTip: Picture the little pointed stick that holds the layers together at 10 Across. A crossing helps with the flat piece of bread at 7 Down.

clues.PICK: Small pointed stick that holds the sandwich layers together
clues.TOMATO: Juicy red fruit often sliced into a club sandwich

notes.PLATE: A broad plate can hold the pieces after a club sandwich is cut. The flat surface keeps the layered pieces easy to pick up.
notes.CRUST: The edges of each toast slice are its crust. Those firmer edges can help a tall club sandwich stay tidy when it is cut into quarters.
notes.TOMATO: A tomato slice adds juice to the layers of a club sandwich. Putting it next to the lettuce can help keep that juice off the toast.

sandwich-counter-4.solvingTip: Look at 5 Across for the metal container the tuna is packed in. It crosses the serving dish that holds the sandwich at 2 Down.

notes.PLATE: The tuna mixture is made in a bowl, then spread on the rye. A plate is what you set the finished sandwich on when you serve it.
notes.SLICE: One slice of rye goes below the tuna and one above it. The word slice describes the flat pieces of bread, while the tuna is the spread between them.
notes.ONION: A little finely chopped onion can give tuna salad a crunch and a sharper taste. Smaller pieces spread through the filling on the rye.

clues.PLATE: Flat dish you serve a tuna sandwich on
clues.SLICE: One flat piece of rye bread for a sandwich
clues.ONION: Layered vegetable sometimes chopped into tuna salad

sandwich-counter-5.solvingTip: Start with the temperature of the meatballs at 2 Down. The crossing at 4 Across asks what the cheese does as it warms on top.
